chunks: From him, from Ibn Fazzal, from Ibn Bukayr, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Whoever intends a good deed, let him hasten to do it and not delay it, for sometimes the servant performs the deed, so Allah, Blessed and Exalted is He, says: 'I have forgiven you and will not write anything against you ever.'

And whoever intends an evil deed, let him not do it, for sometimes the servant performs the evil, so Allah, Glorious is He, sees him and says: 'No, by My Honor and My Majesty, I will not forgive you after it ever.'

key_terms.هَمَّ: Intended or resolved in the heart

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between intending good and intending evil regarding divine forgiveness in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) emphasizes the virtue of immediacy in worship, warning that delaying good deeds risks missing divine forgiveness, while committing evil invites a specific, irrevocable divine decree. This teaching highlights the Shia concept of *tawassul* through good deeds and the delicate balance between hope in mercy and fear of divine justice, urging believers to act on righteous intentions before they are forgotten or overridden by sin.
